title: Least-Privilege by Default: Standardizing Identity-Aware AI Agent Access into a Golden Path
tldr: Least privilege for an agent acting on a user's behalf means every call may do only what both the user and the agent are allowed to do. Hitachi's design builds seven rules into a platform golden path using Keycloak token exchange, SPIFFE/SPIRE attestation, attribute-based policy and Backstage templates, so teams only declare and approve.

key_points.text: MCP made connecting tools easy, but each team secures access its own way (agent's own account, static keys, homemade token checks), causing both vulnerabilities and platform sprawl.
Pillar 1, on whose behalf: keep the user in the sub claim at every hop by exchanging the token for a new one with the next server as audience, instead of passing the first token along.

The common shortcut, client credentials, makes the agent act as itself (a confused deputy); disable agent service accounts in the authorization server and reject tokens without a user at the MCP server.

Pillar 2, which agent: SPIFFE attests the pod (namespace, image digest) and issues a short-lived ID; the authorization server accepts only that, not static client secrets, and writes the agent into the client_id claim.

Pillar 3, what is allowed: the authorization server issues tokens only for approved targets, and the MCP server runs a policy check on both user and agent attributes, e.g. low agent clearance blocks a high-sensitivity payment tool.
A server that skips the audience check accepts tokens meant for another server and defeats target restriction; one team's leaked key can then reach another team's server.
Delivery: three rules live in the authorization server (Keycloak with SPIRE), four in the agent sidecar and server middleware shipped via Backstage templates; teams write only their tools.
Each agent's client is generated from its declaration, not set by hand, because a misconfigured target in the shared layer would affect every agent.
Broad declarations are split into one request per target, each approved by that server's owner, so approval does not pile up in a central team.
Demo: a receipt with a hidden instruction to fetch payroll data fails because Keycloak never issues a payroll token for the expense agent.
Q&A: for SaaS products that do not accept these tokens, an ingress gateway can run the same policy in front of them.

open_gaps.text: Agents with no user behind them are out of scope for this model.
A team can still build a server by hand without the template and skip the audience check.
User identity cannot be propagated into SaaS products that accept only API keys, so their audit logs show a service account.

opportunities.text: Ship MCP server and agent templates with token exchange, audience checks, user-required checks and attribute-based policy built in.
Replace static agent keys with SPIRE-attested workload identity accepted by your authorization server.
Add a declare-and-approve flow where each target server's owner approves agent access and the platform generates the client.
OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange and the confused deputy problem for agents acting on behalf of users.
